alignment.note: Greek uses an articular present participle (οἱ προάγοντες, 'those going before'); Vulgate renders with a relative clause (qui præibant); Syriac employs a demonstrative pronoun plus a relative phrase (ܘܗܢܘܢ ܕܩܕܡܘܗܝ, 'those who [were] before him'), a typical Syriac substantival construction — semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.

Greek οἱ ἀκολουθοῦντες ('those following') is an articular participle; Vulgate again uses a relative clause (qui sequebantur); the Syriac ܘܗܢܘܢ ܕܒܬܪܗ ('those who [were] after him') uses a prepositional/relative construction with the 3ms suffix, supplying the explicit pronominal object absent in the Greek.

Greek ἔκραζον is a single imperfect verb; the Syriac renders the durative aspect periphrastically with the participle ܩܥܝܢ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܘ ('were crying out'), the standard Syriac means of expressing past continuous action, whereas Latin clamabant uses a simple imperfect.
ὡσαννά / ܐܘܫܥܢܐ / Hosanna — all three transliterate the Hebrew/Aramaic acclamation; the Vulgate frames it with colons (10) as direct speech.

Greek substantivises with article plus present participle (ὁ ἐρχόμενος, 'the [One] coming'); Vulgate uses a relative clause with a finite verb (qui venit); Syriac employs the independent pronoun ܗܘ plus a relative finite verb (ܗܘ ܕܐܬܐ, 'he who comes') — equivalent reference, differing syntactic realisation.

Greek and Latin express the locative with a preposition plus noun (ἐν ὀνόματι / in nomine, two words); Syriac compresses this into a single inflected form ܒܫܡܗ ('in his name'), a prefixed preposition with pronominal suffix typical of Syriac morphology.
κυρίου / ܕܡܪܝܐ / Domini — equivalent genitive 'of [the] Lord'; the Vulgate closes the citation with a colon (17).
